cymbospondylus:enwiki:5.title: Cymbospondylus (Specimens that may belong to the genus)

facts.statement: Cymbospondylus lived during the Olenekian to Anisian stages of the Triassic period.
facts.quote: fossil_range: Olenekian-Anisian~

facts.statement: The genus Cymbospondylus was described by Joseph Leidy in 1868.
facts.quote: authority: Leidy, 1868

facts.statement: The first fossils of Cymbospondylus were discovered in the 19th century in Nevada, United States.
facts.quote: The first known fossils of this taxon are a set of more or less complete vertebrae which were discovered in the 19th century in various mountain ranges of Nevada, in the United States, before being named and described by Joseph Leidy in 1868.

facts.statement: More complete fossils of Cymbospondylus were discovered in the early 20th century by University of California expeditions and described by John Campbell Merriam in 1908.
facts.quote: It is in the beginning of the 20th century that more complete fossils were discovered through several expeditions to the Fossil Hill Member launched by the University of California, and described in more detail by John Campbell Merriam in 1908

facts.statement: Recent studies classify Cymbospondylus as the type genus of the family Cymbospondylidae, rather than Shastasauridae.
facts.quote: Cymbospondylus was formerly classified as a representative of the Shastasauridae, but more recent studies consider it to be more basal, view as the type genus of the Cymbospondylidae.

facts.statement: Cymbospondylus is an extinct genus of large ichthyosaurs.
facts.quote: Cymbospondylus (meaning "cupped vertebrae") is an extinct genus of large ichthyosaurs

facts.statement: Cymbospondylus possessed flippers for limbs and a fin on its tail.
facts.quote: As an ichthyosaur, Cymbospondylus had flippers for limbs and a fin on the tail.

facts.statement: The smallest species of Cymbospondylus reached approximately 4 to 5 meters in length.
facts.quote: The different species of Cymbospondylus vary greatly in size, with the smallest reaching around 4 to 5 m in length.

facts.statement: Established species of Cymbospondylus are known from fossil records in Nevada and Switzerland.
facts.quote: All established species of Cymbospondylus are known from the fossil records of Nevada and Switzerland

facts.statement: Cymbospondylus lived in marine ecosystems alongside bivalves, ammonites, Saurichthys, coelacanths, hybodonts, sauropterygians, and other ichthyosaurs.
facts.quote: The formations where the recognized species were discovered show that Cymbospondylus lived in marine ecosystems alongside molluscs like bivalves and ammonites, bony fishes like Saurichthys and coelacanths, cartilaginous fishes like hybodonts, and marine reptiles like sauropterygians and other ichthyosaurs.

facts.statement: Joseph Leidy described Cymbospondylus in 1868 based on vertebrae from Nevada, transmitted by geologist Josiah Dwight Whitney.
facts.quote: In 1868, American paleontologist Joseph Leidy described two new genera of ichthyosaurs dating from the Middle Triassic on the basis of fossil vertebrae discovered in several localities in Nevada, United States, all of which were transmitted through the geologist Josiah Dwight Whitney.

facts.statement: The name Cymbospondylus means "cupped vertebrae" in Ancient Greek, referring to the shape of the vertebrae.
facts.quote: The genus name Cymbospondylus derives from the Ancient Greek words κύμβη (kymbē, "cup") and σπόνδυλος (spondylos, "vertebra"), all taken together literally meaning cupped vertebrae, in reference to the rather obvious shape of this part of the skeleton.

facts.statement: Between 1901 and 1907, the University of California conducted ten expeditions to recover Triassic ichthyosaur fossils in the United States.
facts.quote: Between 1901 and 1907, the University of California sent ten expeditions across different corners of the United States to recover as many ichthyosaur fossils as possible dating from the Triassic

facts.statement: The University of California expeditions collected more than fifty specimens of ichthyosaurs, each preserving significant portions of their skeletons.
facts.quote: The research finally collected more than fifty specimens, each preserving a significant portion of their skeletons.

facts.statement: In 2003, McGowan and Motani argued that the fossils attributed to C. piscosus lack distinctive characteristics to prove its validity.
facts.quote: In their work published in 2003, Christopher McGowan and Ryosuke Motani assert that the fossil vertebrae attributed to C. piscosus do not present distinctive characteristics to prove its validity.

facts.statement: McGowan and Motani suggested that the skeleton UCMP 9950 could be designated as a neotype for C. piscosus to resolve taxonomic issues.
facts.quote: To try to resolve this problem, the two authors suggest that the most complete known skeleton of C. petrinus (UCMP 9950) could be designated as a neotype of C. piscosus.

facts.statement: Because no formal ICZN appeal has been established, the name C. petrinus is retained for the proposed neotype until further notice.
facts.quote: However, as no formal ICZN appeal has been established to date, the name C. petrinus for the proposed neotype should be retained until further notice.

facts.statement: The Swiss specimen PIMUZ T 4351 was formally described in 1989 as Cymbospondylus buchseri by Paul Martin Sander.
facts.quote: The specimen in question, cataloged as PIMUZ T 4351, was formally described for the first time in 1989 under the name C. buchseri by Paul Martin Sander

facts.statement: The species name C. buchseri honors Fritz Buchser, who prepared the holotype skeleton in 1931.
facts.quote: The specific epithet buchseri is named in honor of Fritz Buchser, a member of the Museum of Paleontology at the University of Zurich, the latter having prepared the holotype skeleton in 1931

facts.statement: The species C. nichollsi was described in 2006 by Nadia Fröbisch and colleagues from a skeleton found in the Augusta Mountains.
facts.quote: In 2006, Nadia Fröbisch and colleagues described the species C. nichollsi based on an incomplete skeleton, cataloged as FMNH PR 2251, which was discovered in the Augusta Mountains

facts.statement: The species C. nichollsi is named after Elizabeth Nicholls, a paleontologist specializing in Triassic marine reptiles.
facts.quote: The species in question is named in honor to Elizabeth Nicholls, an American-Canadian paleontologist specializing in Triassic marine reptiles

facts.statement: A new Cymbospondylus fossil was discovered in the Augusta Mountains in 2011 and exhumed in 2014.
facts.quote: In 2011, a notable new Cymbospondylus fossil was also discovered in the Augusta Mountains, then exhumed three years later in 2014

facts.statement: The specimen LACM DI 158109 was formally designated the holotype for C. duelferi in 2020 by Nicole Klein and colleagues.
facts.quote: However, it was only later that the specimen, cataloged as LACM DI 158109, was formally designated a holotype for the species C. duelferi by Nicole Klein and colleagues in 2020

facts.statement: The species name C. duelferi honors Olaf Dülfer, a fossil preparer who contributed to research on Mesozoic marine reptiles.
facts.quote: The species name duelferi was chosen in honor of Olaf Dülfer, fossil preparer who made many practical contributions to research on Mesozoic marine reptiles

facts.statement: Sander discovered a notable Cymbospondylus specimen in the Augusta Mountains in 1998, which was exhumed between 2014 and 2015.
facts.quote: In 1998, still in the Augusta Mountains, Sander discovered another notable specimen of Cymbospondylus, and exhumed it with his colleagues between 2014 and 2015

facts.statement: A new species was named in 2021 from a specimen discovered by Sander in the Augusta Mountains.
facts.quote: It was in 2021, one year after the identification of C. duelferi, that a new species of the genus was named from this specimen in Science by Sander and his colleagues

facts.statement: The species C. youngorum is named after Tom and Bonda Young, who financially supported the fossil exhumation project.
facts.quote: This species, C. youngorum, is named in honor of Tom and Bonda Young, these latter having financially supported the fossil exhumation project

facts.statement: Some specimens of Cymbospondylus from Idaho and Svalbard date to the Olenekian stage of the Lower Triassic.
facts.quote: Three of these specimens, including one from Idaho, and two from the Norwegian archipelago of Svalbard, are dated to the Olenekian stage of the Lower Triassic

facts.statement: An anterior partial skeleton of an ichthyosaur was described by Kuhn-Schnyder in 1980 from Monte Seceda, Italy.
facts.quote: In 1980, Kuhn-Schnyder described an anterior partial skeleton of an ichthyosaur discovered at Monte Seceda, Italy

facts.statement: Sander described two specimens attributed to Cymbospondylus in 1992 from Spitsbergen, Svalbard.
facts.quote: In 1992, Sander described two specimens attributed to Cymbospondylus having been discovered in different localities of Spitsbergen, located in the Norwegian archipelago of Svalbard

facts.statement: Fossils discovered in 1985 in Idaho were referred to Cymbospondylus by Massare and Callaway in 1994.
facts.quote: In 1994, Judy A. Massare and Jack M. Callaway referred to a number of Cymbospondylus fossils discovered in 1985 by H. Gregory McDonald in the Platy Siltstone Member of the Thaynes Formation, in Idaho, United States

facts.statement: Rieppel and Dalla Vecchia attributed two fossils from Forni di Sotto, Italy, with doubt to Cymbospondylus in 2001.
facts.quote: In 2001, Olivier Rieppel and Fabio Marco Dalla Vecchia listed a set of fossils of marine reptiles from the Triassic and having been discovered in the comune of Forni di Sotto, in Italy, including two that they attributed with doubt to Cymbospondylus

facts.statement: Balini and Renesto described four partial vertebrae attributed to Cymbospondylus in 2012 from Piazza Brembana, Italy.
facts.quote: In 2012, Balini and Renesto described four more or less partial vertebrae attributed to Cymbospondylus which were discovered in the comune of Piazza Brembana, in Italy

facts.statement: Numerous vertebrae assigned to the genus were identified in 2013 and 2018 in Svalbard.
facts.quote: In 2013 and 2018, numerous genus-assigned vertebrae were identified in the Vendomdalen Member of the Vikinghøgda Formation, Svalbard

facts.statement: Researchers debated whether a skull attributed to C. petrinus actually belongs to C. nichollsi due to insufficient description of the specimen.
facts.quote: However, as the specimen has been relatively little described in the scientific literature, the authors do not know whether it would show intraspecific variations within C. petrinus, judging therefore that a more in-depth description is necessary

facts.statement: In 1868, Leidy described the species Chonespondylus grandis based on a caudal vertebra fragment found at Star Canyon in the Humboldt Range.
facts.quote: In his 1868 paper describing Cymbospondylus, Leidy also named another ichthyosaur as Chonespondylus grandis, based on a fragment of a caudal vertebra found at Star Canyon in the Humboldt Range.

facts.statement: In 1873, John Whitaker Hulke described the species Ichthyosaurus polaris based on vertebrae and rib fragments found on Isfjorden, Spitsbergen, Norway.
facts.quote: In 1873, John Whitaker Hulke described a species of Ichthyosaurus, I. polaris, named after two sets of vertebrae associated with rib fragments that were discovered on Isfjorden, Spitsbergen, an island in Norway.

facts.statement: While the color of Cymbospondylus is unknown, some early ichthyosaurs may have been uniformly dark-colored, as evidenced by eumelanin pigments found in fossilized skin.
facts.quote: Although the colour of Cymbospondylus is unknown, at least some ichthyosaurs may have been uniformly dark-coloured in life, which is evidenced by the discovery of high concentrations of eumelanin pigments in the preserved skin of an early ichthyosaur fossil.

facts.statement: Merriam expressed hesitation regarding the attribution of I. polaris to Cymbospondylus due to the scarcity of known fossils.
facts.quote: Merriam still expresses some hesitation about this attribution, asserting that the true generic identity cannot be determined for this species due to the few known fossils.

facts.statement: The classification of Guizhouichthyosaurus tangae as a synonym of Shastasaurus was contested in 2010, with some researchers proposing it as a distinct genus.
facts.quote: However, considering that Guizhouichthyosaurus is similar to Shastasaurus, they moved the species as S. tangae. This synonymy was contested the following year, in 2010, in which Michael W. Maisch provisionally reclassified Guizhouichthyosaurus as a distinct genus.

facts.statement: Recent phylogenetic and morphological analyses suggest that Guizhouichthyosaurus is a distinct genus from Shastasaurus.
facts.quote: However, numerous phylogenetic and morphological analyzes subsequently published consider Guizhouichthyosaurus to be distinct genus from Shastasaurus.

facts.statement: The best-known specimen of Cymbospondylus is UCMP 9950, an almost complete skeleton that has been used for size estimates since 1908.
facts.quote: Estimates of the size of C. petrinus have changed relatively little since 1908, mainly due to the almost complete skeleton of specimen UCMP 9950, considered the best known specimen of Cymbospondylus.

facts.statement: Merriam estimated that C. petrinus exceeded 9.1 meters in length based on specimens UCMP 9947 and 9950.
facts.quote: Merriam suggests that C. petrinus would reach a size exceeding 9.1 m in length based on specimens UCMP 9947 and 9950.

facts.statement: In 2020, Klein and colleagues estimated C. petrinus at 9.3 meters long for a skull measuring 1.16 meters.
facts.quote: In 2020, Klein and colleagues increased the size estimate of C. petrinus a little further, seeing them as reaching 9.3 m for a 1.16 m skull.

facts.statement: In 2021, Sander and colleagues estimated C. petrinus at 12.56 meters long and approximately 5.7 metric tons in weight.
facts.quote: In 2021, Sander and is colleagues in 2021 estimates C. petrinus to 12.56 m long for about 5.7 MT, while keeping the same cranial measurements.

facts.statement: C. youngorum is estimated to reach a maximum length of 17.65 meters and a weight of 44.7 metric tons, based on a skull nearly 2 meters long and a large humerus.
facts.quote: The holotype specimen of C. youngorum having a skull measuring almost 2 m long and its humerus being the second largest bone of this type recorded in an ichthyosaur, the maximum size of the animal is therefore estimated at 17.65 m for a weight of 44.7 MT.

facts.statement: C. youngorum is considered one of the largest ichthyosaurs known, second only to Ichthyotitan, and one of the largest animals of its time.
facts.quote: This estimate not only makes C. youngourum one of the largest ichthyosaurians identified to date behind Ichthyotitan, but also makes it one of the largest animals known of its time.

facts.statement: Researchers Lene Liebe Delsett and Nicholas David Pyenson describe C. youngorum as "the first aquatic giant" due to its early Middle Triassic age and large size.
facts.quote: The antiquity as well as such an imposing size for an animal dating from the beginning of the Middle Triassic makes C. youngorum qualify as "the first aquatic giant" according to Lene Liebe Delsett and Nicholas David Pyenson.

facts.statement: C. nichollsi is estimated to be 7.6 meters long with a skull length of 97 centimeters and a body mass of 3 metric tons.
facts.quote: However, based on the comparison with C. buchseri and C. petrinus, the total length of the skull is estimated at 97 cm for an animal measuring 7.6 m long, all for a body mass of 3 MT.

facts.statement: C. buchseri is estimated to be 5 to 5.5 meters long with a 68-centimeter skull, though its weight has not been estimated.
facts.quote: The estimated size of the C. buchseri holotype is slightly shorter, reaching a length of 5 to 5.5 m with a skull 68 cm long, although no estimate of its weight has yet been published.

facts.statement: In 2021, Sander and colleagues re-estimated C. duelferi at around 5 meters long and 520 kilograms in weight.
facts.quote: The measurements of the species are estimated again at around 5 m for a body mass of 520 kg by Sander and colleagues in 2021.

facts.statement: Specimen IGPB R660 from the Vikinghøgda Formation is estimated to be 7.5 to 9.5 meters long, making it the largest known Lower Triassic ichthyosaur.
facts.quote: Using the same measurement technique as those done for C. youngorum, a specimen cataloged as IGPB R660, known from the Vikinghøgda Formation, has an estimated size between 7.5 to 9.5 m long, making it the largest known ichthyosaur specimen from the Lower Triassic.

facts.statement: Cymbospondylus has an elongated, conical snout where the premaxillae and nasal bones are the largest.
facts.quote: Like other ichthyosaurs, the snout of Cymbospondylus is elongated into a long, conical rostrum, the largest bones of which are the premaxillae and nasal bones.

facts.statement: In Cymbospondylus, the nasal bones extend backward to the anterior edge of the temporal fenestrae along with the frontal bones.
facts.quote: The nasal bones also extend far back, and, with the frontal bones, reach the anterior edge of the temporal fenestrae.

facts.statement: The eye sockets of Cymbospondylus are oval to ovoid and proportionally small relative to the skull size.
facts.quote: The eye sockets are oval to ovoid in shape and are proportionally small in relation to the size of the skull.

facts.statement: The superior temporal fenestra is oval in C. nichollsi and C. duelferi but triangular in C. petrinus.
facts.quote: The shape of the superior temporal fenestra differs between some species, being oval in C. nichollsi and C. duelferi but triangular in C. petrinus.

facts.statement: The scleral ring ossicle count varies by species: 12 in C. duelferi, 13 in C. buchseri, 14 in C. nichollsi, and 14 to 18 in C. petrinus.
facts.quote: The number of bony elements constituting the scleral rings varies between species: 12 ossicles in C. duelferi; 13 ossicles in C. buchseri; 14 ossicles in C. nichollsi; and between 14 and 18 ossicles in C. petrinus.

facts.statement: The sagittal crest is low in C. duelferi and C. nichollsi, high in C. petrinus, and absent in C. youngorum.
facts.quote: The sagittal crest is more or less pronounced in the different species, being low in C. duelferi and C. nichollsi, clearly high in C. petrinus, and totally absent in C. youngorum.

facts.statement: The occipital condyle of Cymbospondylus is concave.
facts.quote: The occipital condyle of Cymbospondylus is concave in shape.

facts.statement: Cymbospondylus possesses an elongated and thin lower jaw that extends beyond the back of the skull.
facts.quote: Like other ichthyosaurs, Cymbospondylus has an elongated and thin lower jaw, extending backwards to beyond the back of the skull.

facts.statement: C. petrinus exhibits a unique thecodont dentition where teeth appear fused at the bottom of the alveoli.
facts.quote: C. petrinus has a particular form of thecodont dentition, its teeth appearing to be fused at the bottom of the alveoli.

facts.statement: C. duelferi has subthecodont dentition, with teeth implanted in shallow sockets.
facts.quote: C. duelferi has a subthecodont type of dentition, meaning that its teeth are implanted in shallow sockets.

facts.statement: C. youngorum has a thick bone base attaching to the teeth, a trait not found in other ichthyosaurs.
facts.quote: C. youngorum has a thick base of the bone attaching to the teeth, a trait not seen in other ichthyosaurs.

facts.statement: Cymbospondylus teeth are homodont, sharing an identical conical, ridged, and pointed shape.
facts.quote: The teeth are homodont, that is to say they share an identical shape, being conical, ridged and pointed.

facts.statement: Cymbospondylus teeth feature longitudinal ridges extending from the crown base to the apical third.
facts.quote: The teeth also have longitudinal ridges that extend from the base of the crown to the apical third.

facts.statement: Tooth counts are known for three species: C. duelferi has over 21 upper jaw teeth, C. petrinus has 30 to 35 teeth in both jaws, and C. youngorum has 43 upper and over 31 lower jaw teeth.
facts.quote: Only three species were able to have a more or less clear estimate of their number of teeth: C. duelferi having a number greater than 21 teeth known in the upper jaw, but unknown in the lower jaw; C. petrinus with between 30 and 35 teeth in the upper and lower jaws; and C. youngorum having 43 teeth in the upper jaw and more than 31 teeth in the lower jaw.

facts.statement: It is agreed that Cymbospondylus is a basal member of the Ichthyosauria clade.
facts.quote: However it is agreed upon that Cymbospondylus is a rather basal member of the clade.

facts.statement: In a 2021 analysis, Cymbospondylus was placed at the base of Ichthyosauria, outside the derived Hueneosauria group.
facts.quote: In the analysis of Bindellini et al. (2021), Cymbospondylus is placed at the very base of Ichthyosauria, outside the more derived members of Hueneosauria (including Mixosauridae and Shastasauridae).

facts.statement: C. youngorum is considered the most derived member of a Nevada clade, while C. buchseri sits at the base of the genus.
facts.quote: The description of C. youngorum further supports this Nevadan clade, recovering C. youngorum as its most derived member while C. buchseri from Europe sits at the base of the genus.

facts.statement: The convoluted taxonomy of Cymbospondylus has led some to suggest neglecting the type species due to its fragmentary nature.
facts.quote: The type species was not included in the dataset due to its questionable and fragmentary nature. This causes Cymbospondylus to have a very convoluted taxonomy, with it being suggested that the type species should be neglected.

facts.statement: C. youngorum dates from the beginning of the Middle Triassic.
facts.quote: The antiquity as well as such an imposing size for an animal dating from the beginning of the Middle Triassic makes C. youngorum qualify as "the first aquatic giant" according to Lene Liebe Delsett and Nicholas David Pyenson.

facts.statement: Cymbospondylus lived in what is now North America and Europe during the middle Triassic period.
facts.quote: Cymbospondylus es un ictiosaurio que vivió en lo que hoy es Norteamérica y Europa a mediados del período Triásico.

facts.statement: Fossils of Cymbospondylus have been found in North America and Europe.
facts.quote: Cymbospondylus es un ictiosaurio que vivió en lo que hoy es Norteamérica y Europa a mediados del período Triásico.

facts.statement: Cymbospondylus had two pairs of flippers and an eel-like tail, and lacked a dorsal fin.
facts.quote: Este reptil marino tenía 2 pares de aletas y una cola parecida a la de las anguilas y debido a ser uno de los primeros reptiles marinos ictiosauros, era el ictiosaurio menos parecido a los peces ya que este no poseía la aleta dorsal

facts.statement: Cymbospondylus reached an approximate length of 6 to 10 meters.
facts.quote: con una longitud aproximada de 6 a 10 metros

facts.statement: Cymbospondylus had a curved skull with sharp teeth used to eat reptiles, primitive amphibians, and cephalopods like Ammonites.
facts.quote: Su cráneo era curvado y tenía dientes afilados para comer reptiles, anfibios primitivos y cefalópodos tales como el Ammonites

facts.statement: The genus Cymbospondylus was described by Leidy in 1868.
facts.quote: genus_authority: Leidy, 1868

facts.statement: Cymbospondylus belongs to the family Cymbospondylidae.
facts.quote: familia: Cymbospondylidae

facts.statement: Cymbospondylus is classified as a genus within the order Ichthyosauria.
facts.quote: genus: Cymbospondylus

facts.statement: It is suggested that Cymbospondylus fossils found in Nevada and Switzerland are ancestral to most streamlined Cretaceous ichthyosaurs.
facts.quote: Sus fósiles han sido hallados en Nevada (EE. UU.) y Suiza de este espécimen descienden la mayoría de los ictiosauros más estilizados del Cretácico.
